passages.happening:
“Then Pilate took Jesus and had Him flogged” (verse 1). The soldiers twist a crown of thorns, put it on his head, dress him in a purple robe, and come up to him again and again, saying, “Hail, King of the Jews!” and slapping him (verses 2-3).

Pilate comes out again and says he finds no basis for a charge against him (verse 4). Jesus comes out wearing the crown and the robe, and Pilate says, “Here is the man!” (verse 5).

As soon as the chief priests and officers see him, they shout, “Crucify Him! Crucify Him!” (verse 6). Pilate tells them to crucify him themselves, for he finds no case against him. They answer, “We have a law,” and say that by that law he must die, “because He declared Himself to be the Son of God” (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
The Mark 15 note tells of the flogging and the soldiers' mockery, and John adds little to it. In Mark and Matthew the flogging comes after the sentence. In John it comes in the middle of the trial, and Pilate seems to use it as a half-measure, as if a beaten man might satisfy the accusers and let him go free.

Then he shows Jesus to them: “Here is the man!” In the Latin Bible the words are Ecce homo, and countless paintings carry that title. Pilate may mean it with scorn or with pity: look at this harmless, broken man; is this a king? John wants the reader to hear more. Here is the man, the true human being, the Word who became flesh (1:14), showing what God is like by what he is willing to suffer.

John is careful to say who shouts ‘Crucify’: ‘the chief priests and officers’, the temple authorities and their police. This is what John often means by ‘the Jews’ in the trial, and verse 7 uses that phrase for the same people. The book page explains it in ‘The Jews in John’.

Verse 7 brings out the real charge. To Pilate they had spoken of a king. Now they say he claimed to be the Son of God. In their eyes that was blasphemy, a crime the law of Moses punished with death.
passages.ot:
The law said, “Whoever blasphemes the name of the LORD must surely be put to death” (Leviticus 24:16). The leaders believed they were obeying it. John has shown all along why they thought Jesus blasphemed: he called God his own Father, “making Himself equal with God” (5:18).

Isaiah's servant was beaten and despised: “He was pierced for our transgressions, He was crushed for our iniquities; the punishment that brought us peace was upon Him, and by His stripes we are healed” (Isaiah 53:5). The church has always read this chapter of Isaiah in the light of this morning.
passages.hard:
Is John saying the Jewish people wanted Jesus dead? No. He names the people who shouted: the chief priests and their officers. The crowds who had welcomed Jesus a few days before were Jews (12:12-13), as were Jesus, his mother and his disciples. The note on 19:13-16 below faces the long misuse of this scene in full.

Is Pilate the innocent one, then? John does not say so either. Three times Pilate says he finds no case against Jesus (18:38, 19:4, 19:6), and he has him flogged anyway. A judge who knows a man is innocent and has him whipped is not innocent himself.
passages.asks: ‘Here is the man.’ Pilate showed the crowd a beaten prisoner in a mock crown, and Christians have looked at that picture ever since. Ask what you see. A failed king? Or the clearest picture of what God is like, a love that will take the worst we can do? And notice Pilate, who knew the truth and did the wrong thing anyway. Ask where you know what is right and are looking for a way around it.

passages.t: Where are You from? The greater sin
passages.happening:
When Pilate hears that Jesus claimed to be the Son of God, “he was even more afraid” (verse 8). He goes back inside and asks Jesus, “Where are You from?” Jesus gives no answer (verse 9).

“Do You refuse to speak to me?” Pilate says. “Do You not know that I have authority to release You and authority to crucify You?” (verse 10).

Jesus answers, “You would have no authority over Me if it were not given to you from above. Therefore the one who handed Me over to you is guilty of greater sin” (verse 11).

From then on Pilate tries to release him. But the accusers keep shouting, “If you release this man, you are no friend of Caesar. Anyone who declares himself a king is defying Caesar” (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
Why is Pilate afraid? In his world many people believed that gods could walk the earth in human form. When Paul healed a man in Lystra, the crowd cried, “The gods have come down to us in human form!” (Acts 14:11). Pilate may have wondered whom he was dealing with. His question, ‘Where are You from?’, is the question John's whole book has been asking (7:27-28, 8:14). The reader knows the answer: from the Father.

Pilate boasts of his authority. Jesus tells him where it comes from: ‘from above’. Pilate is a real ruler with real power, but he answers to God for how he uses it.

‘No friend of Caesar’ was a sharp threat. ‘Friend of Caesar’ seems to have been an honor given to men the emperor trusted, and some scholars think it was something like an official title. To be reported to the emperor Tiberius as ‘no friend of Caesar’, a governor who let a rival king go free, could end a career, or a life. Some scholars connect Pilate's fear with the fall of the powerful Roman officer Sejanus in AD 31, who may have helped him to his post. Others think no such link is needed. The threat was dangerous either way.

In verse 12 ‘the Jews’ who shout are the same chief priests and officers named in verse 6.
passages.ot:
The prophets taught that God gives rulers their power and can take it away. Daniel told a king that “the Most High rules over the kingdom of mankind” (Daniel 4:17). A psalm pictures the rulers of the earth gathering “against the LORD and against His Anointed One” (Psalm 2:2). Jesus stands before such a ruler and tells him calmly that his authority was lent to him.

Isaiah said of the servant, “He was oppressed and afflicted, yet He did not open His mouth” (Isaiah 53:7). Jesus' silence in verse 9 fits that picture.
passages.hard:
Who is ‘the one who handed Me over’, guilty of ‘greater sin’? Readers have given different answers. Many think Jesus means Caiaphas, the high priest who sent him to Pilate (18:24, 18:28). Others think he means Judas, whom John calls ‘the one who handed Him over’ again and again (the same Greek verb is used of him). Some think the words take in all who handed him over.

Notice what Jesus does not say. He does not say Pilate is innocent. He says Pilate's sin is less, because Pilate did not start this and knows less than those who did. Sin is real on every side of this trial. Responsibility depends on what each person knew and chose.

And notice what the verse does not say about a people. It speaks of one person, ‘the one who handed Me over’. It gives no one any ground for blaming a nation.
passages.asks: Pilate thought his power was his own. Jesus told him it was on loan. Ask what authority you hold, over children, workers, a household, a church, and whether you use it as one who must give an account. And notice the threat that moved Pilate: what would people say about his loyalty? Ask what fear of losing your standing has made you do.

passages.t: We have no king but Caesar
passages.happening:
When Pilate hears this, he brings Jesus out and sits down on the judgment seat at a place called the Stone Pavement, “which in Hebrew is Gabbatha” (verse 13).

John notes the time: “It was the day of Preparation for the Passover, about the sixth hour.” Pilate says to the accusers, “Here is your King!” (verse 14).

They shout, “Away with Him! Away with Him! Crucify Him!” Pilate asks, “Shall I crucify your King?” And the chief priests answer, “We have no king but Caesar” (verse 15).

“Then Pilate handed Jesus over to be crucified, and the soldiers took Him away” (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
The judgment seat was where a Roman governor sat to give an official sentence. Where the Stone Pavement was depends on where the Praetorium was, which scholars still debate (see 18:28). A paved area shown to visitors near the old Antonia fortress was laid down later than Jesus' day, most archaeologists think.

John gives a day and an hour. The day is ‘the day of Preparation for the Passover’, the day the Passover lambs were killed in the temple in the afternoon. In John's account Jesus is sentenced around noon on that day, so he dies while the lambs are being killed. John the Baptist had called him “the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world” (1:29).

Mark tells it differently. He presents the Last Supper as the Passover meal itself, and he says Jesus was crucified at ‘the third hour’, about nine in the morning (Mark 15:25). The note on Mark 14 sets out the answers Christians have given on the day. Some argue that John's words refer to other meals and the Friday of the feast week, so that John and Mark agree. Some suggest different groups kept different calendars. Some think Jesus held a farewell meal full of Passover meaning on the evening before. And some think one Gospel arranged the timing to make a point, John to show Jesus as the Passover lamb. No answer has won general agreement.

On the hour, too, there are several answers. John says ‘about’ the sixth hour, and some think both writers are giving round figures for the same late morning. Some think John counted hours from midnight, so that his sixth hour is six in the morning, though others doubt that John counted this way. Some suggest a copyist's slip, and a few old copies of John do read ‘third hour’, but the best copies read ‘sixth’, as the Berean Standard Bible does. These notes take no side. All four Gospels agree that Jesus died at Passover time, on a Friday, and that his death is to be understood in the light of the exodus.
passages.ot:
Israel's faith was that God himself was their king. When Gideon was asked to found a royal line, he said, “The LORD shall rule over you” (Judges 8:23). When the people first asked for a king, God told Samuel, “it is not you they have rejected, but they have rejected Me as their king” (1 Samuel 8:7). Isaiah sang, “the LORD is our King. It is He who will save us” (Isaiah 33:22).

That is the weight of what the chief priests say. The leaders of God's temple, of all people, confess no king but the Roman emperor.
passages.hard:
‘We have no king but Caesar’ was said by the chief priests, not by the Jewish people. John names them on purpose. The speakers were the temple's rulers, men who held office by Rome's leave, and the cry was theirs on one morning in one courtyard. It was not the voice of Jesus' own disciples, nor of the crowds who had welcomed him, nor of Jewish people then living in Galilee, Rome or Babylon, nor of any Jew since.

This is the place where John's passion story has been misused most cruelly, so it should be said here in full. For centuries many Christians called the Jewish people ‘Christ-killers’ and used scenes like this to justify contempt, expulsions, and violence against Jews. That reading is false, and Christians must reject it plainly. This site rejects it. Jesus himself, his disciples, and the crowds who welcomed him were Jews. A Roman governor gave the order, and Roman soldiers carried it out. In 1965 the Catholic Church's Second Vatican Council said that what happened in the passion ‘cannot be charged against all the Jews, without distinction, then alive, nor against the Jews of today’. Most churches teach the same. The New Testament places all people inside the guilt: in Acts the first Christians pray that Herod, Pilate, the Gentiles, and the people of Israel all stood together against Jesus (Acts 4:27).

And John's own book puts every reader inside it. ‘The world’ did not recognize him (1:10). The chief priests chose Caesar to keep their power. Christians have done the same thing many times since: traded loyalty to Jesus for safety with whoever held power. The cry ‘no king but Caesar’ is a warning to the church, not a charge against a people.
passages.asks: When it came to the point, the leaders chose the emperor over the King standing in front of them, because the emperor could protect their place. Ask who your Caesar is: the power, party, money or approval you would choose over Jesus if you had to. Every Christian has faced that choice. Not every Christian has chosen well.

passages.t: What I have written, I have written
passages.happening:
“Carrying His own cross, He went out to The Place of the Skull, which in Hebrew is called Golgotha” (verse 17). “There they crucified Him, and with Him two others, one on each side, with Jesus in the middle” (verse 18).

Pilate has a notice fixed to the cross: JESUS OF NAZARETH, THE KING OF THE JEWS (verse 19). Many people read it, because the place is near the city, and it is written in Hebrew, Latin and Greek (verse 20).

The chief priests object. They want it to say only that he claimed to be the King of the Jews (verse 21). Pilate answers, “What I have written, I have written” (verse 22).
passages.hearers:
Crucifixion was a Roman punishment for slaves, rebels, and violent criminals. The note on Mark 15 tells what is known of it. John, like the other Gospels, does not dwell on the pain. He says only, ‘There they crucified Him.’

The other Gospels say that Simon of Cyrene was made to carry the cross (Mark 15:21). John says Jesus carried it himself. Many readers think both are true: Jesus set out carrying the crossbeam, and on the way, too weak to go on, he was helped. John chooses to show Jesus going out under his own load.

A notice naming the crime was often carried before a condemned man or fixed to his cross. Only John says it was in three languages. Hebrew here probably means the Aramaic spoken by Jews of the land. Latin was the language of Roman power and law. Greek was the common language of the eastern Mediterranean. So the notice spoke to everyone in the city. In Latin it reads Iesus Nazarenus Rex Iudaeorum, and its first letters, INRI, are carved on many crosses today.

Pilate may have meant the notice as a jab at the chief priests who had forced his hand. John sees the truth inside it. The King of the Jews is announced to the world in the world's languages, from a cross.
passages.ot:
When Abraham was told to offer his son, “Abraham took the wood for the burnt offering and placed it on his son Isaac” (Genesis 22:6). Many readers since the early church have seen Jesus carrying his own cross in that picture, though John does not draw the line himself.

Isaiah said the servant would be “lifted up and highly exalted” (Isaiah 52:13), and that God would make him “a light for the nations” (Isaiah 49:6). The notice in three languages does both.
passages.hard: Why does John say Jesus carried his own cross, when Mark says Simon carried it? John does not deny that Simon helped. He leaves him out. Many readers think John wanted to show that Jesus went to his death of his own accord, as he said: “No one takes it from Me, but I lay it down of My own accord” (10:18). Others have noticed the echo of Isaac carrying the wood. The two accounts are easy to fit together, and John's choice tells us what he wanted his readers to see.
passages.asks: The chief priests wanted the notice changed to ‘He said he was king.’ Pilate refused. So for all to read, in every language of the city, the cross said: this is the King. Ask whether you believe the notice, or only that he claimed it. And ask what kind of King reigns from a cross.

passages.t: The seamless tunic, and his mother
passages.happening:
The soldiers divide Jesus' clothes into four parts, one for each soldier. His tunic is left, “seamless, woven in one piece from top to bottom” (verse 23). So they say, “Let us not tear it. Instead, let us cast lots to see who will get it.” John says this fulfilled the Scripture: “They divided My garments among them, and cast lots for My clothing” (verse 24).

Near the cross stand his mother, her sister, Mary the wife of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene (verse 25).

Jesus sees his mother and the disciple whom he loved standing nearby. He says to his mother, “Woman, here is your son.” Then he says to the disciple, “Here is your mother.” And from that hour the disciple takes her into his home (verses 26-27).
passages.hearers:
A crucified man was stripped, and his clothes went to the soldiers who did the work. Four soldiers, four shares. The tunic, the long garment worn next to the skin, was too good to cut up.

Why does John mention that it was seamless? He does not say. Some readers note that Josephus describes the high priest's long garment as woven in one piece, not made of two, and they see Jesus as the true high priest, the one who prayed in chapter 17. Others note that John's word is the ordinary word for a tunic, and doubt any hidden meaning. Many Christians have also seen the untorn tunic as a picture of the church's unity, the oneness Jesus prayed for (17:21). These are readings, and John leaves them to the reader.

The women stayed. The note on Mark 15 says it simply: the men have run away; the women stay. John adds Jesus' mother, and he alone tells of the beloved disciple standing with them.

‘Woman’ was not cold or rude. As the note on 2:4 explains, it was a respectful way to speak to a woman. And notice that Jesus' last care, in his own agony, is for his mother's future. A widow, it seems, about to lose her eldest son, she would need a home. He gives her one.
passages.ot:
John quotes a psalm: “They divide my garments among them and cast lots for my clothing” (Psalm 22:18). Psalm 22 is the psalm that begins, ‘My God, my God, why have You forsaken me?’, the cry Mark and Matthew record from the cross. It is the prayer of a righteous sufferer surrounded by enemies, and it ends in praise. The Gospel writers saw the whole psalm come true in Jesus.

The law commanded, “Honor your father and mother” (Exodus 20:12). Jesus keeps that command from the cross.

When Jesus was a baby, the old man Simeon told Mary that a sword would pierce her own soul (Luke 2:35). Here it does.
passages.hard:
Why give his mother to the disciple, and not to his brothers? John has said that Jesus' brothers did not yet believe in him (7:5). Many readers think Jesus entrusted her to a believer. Others think the beloved disciple may have been a relative, but that rests on guesses about the Gospels' lists of women, and no one can be sure.

The scene has been read in more than one way. Catholic and Orthodox Christians often see in it Mary given as a mother to all disciples, whom the beloved disciple stands for. Many Protestants read it chiefly as a son's care for his mother. Both readings honor what is plainly there: love that kept working to the end.

And this scene is for every parent who has watched a child suffer or die. Mary stood there. The Gospel does not tell us what she felt, and it does not hurry her away. If you have lost a child, or carry a grief like hers, please do not carry it alone. Speak to someone you trust, a pastor or a grief counsellor, and if the pain ever feels like more than you can bear, reach out today to a crisis line or emergency service.
passages.asks: In the worst hour of his life Jesus made sure his mother would be looked after. Ask whom you are responsible for, and whether your own troubles have made you forget them. And notice what he did: he made a family out of two grieving people. Ask who near you is grieving and alone, and whether you could become their family for a while.

passages.t: I am thirsty. It is finished
passages.happening:
Jesus knows “that everything had now been accomplished”. And to fulfill the Scripture, he says, “I am thirsty” (verse 28).

A jar of sour wine stands there. They soak a sponge in it, put it on a stalk of hyssop, and lift it to his mouth (verse 29).

When he has received the sour wine, he says, “It is finished.” Then, “bowing His head, He yielded up His spirit” (verse 30).
passages.hearers:
The sour wine was cheap wine gone sharp, the common drink of soldiers and workers. It was not a cruelty here; someone gave a dying man a drink.

‘I am thirsty’ is the most human sentence Jesus speaks from the cross in John. The Word who was with God in the beginning (1:1) is thirsty. Early in the book he asked a Samaritan woman for water, and promised her living water (4:7-14). Now he thirsts again, and no one in the story has living water to give him.

‘It is finished’ is one word in Greek, tetelestai. It comes from the verb ‘to finish, complete, carry out’. John uses the same word two verses earlier: Jesus knew ‘that everything had now been accomplished’. The work the Father gave him is done (17:4). It is not the gasp of a defeated man. It is the word of someone who has finished what he came to do.

Then ‘He yielded up His spirit’, literally ‘he handed over the spirit’. John does not say his life was taken. Jesus gives it. And the verb is the one John has used again and again for the handing over of Jesus himself: Judas handed him over, the priests handed him over, Pilate handed him over. Now Jesus hands over his own spirit to the Father.
passages.ot:
A psalm of the righteous sufferer says, “They poisoned my food with gall and gave me vinegar to quench my thirst” (Psalm 69:21). Another says, “my tongue sticks to the roof of my mouth” (Psalm 22:15). John says Jesus spoke ‘to fulfill the Scripture’.

The hyssop is a small detail with a long history. On the night of the first Passover in Egypt, Israel was told, “Take a cluster of hyssop, dip it into the blood in the basin, and brush the blood on the top and sides of the doorframe” (Exodus 12:22). In John, Jesus is the Passover lamb, and hyssop is lifted to him at his death. Some readers ask whether a hyssop stalk was strong enough to hold a soaked sponge, and suggest it was tied to a reed; John does not explain. But he did not mention hyssop by chance.
passages.hard: What does ‘It is finished’ mean? Christians have heard in it the finishing of everything Jesus came to do: the Father's work completed (17:4), the Scriptures fulfilled, the sacrifice for sin made once for all, as the letter to the Hebrews later puts it (Hebrews 10:10). Christians differ on how best to describe what the cross achieved, and these notes do not set out a full theory. All agree that what God set out to do in the death of his Son, he did. Nothing was left half done.
passages.asks: Jesus said ‘It is finished’ about his work. Many of us live as if his work were not quite finished, as if we must add something to make God accept us. Ask what you are still trying to pay that he has already paid. And notice that the one who finished the work of salvation also said ‘I am thirsty’. He was not too holy to need a drink. He is not too holy to understand your need.

passages.t: Not one of His bones will be broken
passages.happening:
It is the day of Preparation, and the next day is “a High Sabbath”. So that the bodies will not stay on the crosses over the Sabbath, the authorities ask Pilate to have the legs broken and the bodies taken down (verse 31).

The soldiers break the legs of the two men crucified with Jesus. When they come to Jesus and see that he is already dead, they do not break his legs (verses 32-33). “Instead, one of the soldiers pierced His side with a spear, and immediately blood and water flowed out” (verse 34).

John stops to say that the one who saw it has testified, “and his testimony is true”, so that the reader may believe (verse 35). He gives two Scriptures: “Not one of His bones will be broken” (verse 36) and “They will look on the One they have pierced” (verse 37).
passages.hearers:
The law of Moses said that the body of an executed man must not be left hanging overnight (Deuteronomy 21:23). This Sabbath was a ‘High Sabbath’, because it fell during the Passover feast. Romans could leave bodies on crosses for days as a warning. In Judea the authorities asked for them to be taken down.

Breaking the legs hastened death, since a crucified man could no longer push himself up. Scholars debate exactly how crucifixion killed, and these notes do not go further into it. What matters to John is that Jesus was already dead.

The spear made sure. A soldier, trained to know death when he saw it, struck the body, and blood and water came out. John insists that this was seen by an eyewitness whose word is true. He wants no one to say that Jesus only fainted.

In verse 31 ‘the Jews’ who ask Pilate are the authorities, keeping the law about bodies and the Sabbath, as verse 38 shows.
passages.ot:
‘Not one of His bones will be broken’ points back to the Passover lamb. God said of the lamb, “you may not break any of the bones” (Exodus 12:46; also Numbers 9:12). It also echoes a psalm about the righteous man: “He protects all his bones; not one of them will be broken” (Psalm 34:20). For John, Jesus is both: the righteous one God protects, and the true Passover lamb.

‘They will look on the One they have pierced’ comes from Zechariah. There God promises to pour out “a spirit of grace and prayer” on Jerusalem, and the people “will look on Me, the One they have pierced. They will mourn for Him as one mourns for an only child” (Zechariah 12:10). In Zechariah the looking leads to mourning, and the next chapter speaks of a fountain opened to cleanse from sin (Zechariah 13:1). Looking at the pierced one is the start of repentance and healing.
passages.hard:
What do the blood and water mean? John does not say, and Christians have read it in several ways, which can sit together.

Some read it first as plain evidence: a real body, really dead. Many have tried to explain it medically, though no one can be sure what a doctor would say about a body they never saw.

Many early Christian teachers saw the church's sacraments in it. Augustine, reading a Latin Bible that says the side was ‘opened’, saw the blood and water as baptism and the Lord's Supper flowing from it. He and John Chrysostom both compared it to Eve, made from the side of the sleeping Adam (Genesis 2:21-22): the church, the bride, comes from the side of Christ.

Others connect it with Jesus' promise that rivers of living water would flow from within, which John explains as the Spirit (7:38-39). And many think John's first letter speaks of Jesus as the one who came “by water and blood” (1 John 5:6), against teachers who said Christ only seemed to be a real man.

These readings do not compete for the truth of the event. John's main point is clear. The death was real, and from it life flows.
passages.asks: John wants you to look at the one who was pierced. Not with a quick glance, but the way Zechariah meant: with grief, and with hope of cleansing. Ask what you see when you look. And notice how carefully John says that someone saw this and told the truth. Your faith does not rest on a feeling. It rests on a witness who was there.

passages.t: Joseph, Nicodemus, and a new tomb
passages.happening:
Afterward Joseph of Arimathea, “who was a disciple of Jesus (but secretly for fear of the Jews)”, asks Pilate for the body. Pilate allows it, and Joseph takes the body away (verse 38).

Nicodemus, who had first come to Jesus at night, comes too, bringing a mixture of myrrh and aloes, “about seventy-five pounds” (verse 39). They wrap the body in linen cloths with the spices, as Jewish burial custom was (verse 40).

There is a garden near the place of the crucifixion, and in it a new tomb where no one had yet been laid. Because it is the day of Preparation and the tomb is near, they lay Jesus there (verses 41-42).
passages.hearers:
The note on Mark 15 tells of Joseph: a respected member of the council, who took his courage in his hands and went to Pilate. John adds that he had been a disciple in secret, ‘for fear of the Jews’. Here the phrase means the authorities, the council he belonged to, whose anger he had reason to fear. Joseph and Nicodemus were Jews and members of that council themselves.

Nicodemus has appeared twice before. He came to Jesus at night with questions (3:2). Later he spoke up in the council for a fair hearing (7:50-51). Now he comes in daylight, to a crucified man, with an enormous gift.

The Greek says a hundred litrai, a Roman measure of weight of about a third of a kilogram, so about 33 kilograms. That is far more than any burial needed. Many readers think John is telling us that Jesus was buried like a king, the King of the notice on the cross.

Jewish burial did not embalm the body as Egyptians did. The body was washed and wrapped in linen with spices, and laid in a tomb. The note on Mark 16 says more. The tomb was new, cut in rock, and close by, in a garden.
passages.ot:
Isaiah said of the servant, “He was assigned a grave with the wicked, and with a rich man in His death” (Isaiah 53:9). Matthew tells us Joseph was rich (Matthew 27:57).

When King Asa of Judah died, “They laid him on a bier that was full of spices and various blended perfumes” (2 Chronicles 16:14). Great amounts of spices could mark a royal or honored burial. The garden, too, may recall the first garden in Genesis. John begins his book ‘In the beginning’, and he ends the story of the cross in a garden, where new creation is about to break in.
passages.hard:
Was Jesus really buried in a tomb, or is the burial a later legend? Some scholars have argued that crucified men were usually left unburied or thrown into common graves, and that the tomb story grew later. Others reply that Jewish custom and the law of Moses required burial the same day (Deuteronomy 21:23), and that archaeology has found at least one crucified man, Yehohanan, buried in his family's tomb, as the note on Mark 15 explains. And it would be strange for Christians to invent a burial by a member of the very council that condemned Jesus.

All four Gospels tell of Joseph, and Paul, writing in the 50s, repeats the early teaching that Christ died, “that He was buried, that He was raised on the third day” (1 Corinthians 15:4). These notes hold, with the creeds, that he was crucified, died, and was buried.
passages.asks: Joseph and Nicodemus were secret believers. Both had held back for fear. On the darkest day, when everything seemed lost and there was nothing left to gain, they came out into the open. Ask where you have kept your faith quiet for fear of what it would cost. It is not too late to step forward. For them, it was the day after everything seemed over that they finally did.
